title: Marisma: Manage a Wetland
subtitle: Manage a Mediterranean wetland for 20 years — and discover why short-term wins can cause long-term collapse.
module: High School — Introduction to the course

learningFocus.summary: Students take charge of a whole ecosystem — a Mediterranean wetland — and manage it for twenty years on a fixed annual budget, watching a living food web respond to every decision. In doing so they practise the foundational ideas of Environmental Science in one connected system: energy flow through a food web, carrying capacity and limiting factors, nutrient pollution and eutrophication, invasive species, habitat loss, and the difference between immediate and delayed consequences. Crucially, they weigh genuine trade-offs between conservation, farming, housing and tourism — there is no single right answer — and must defend their strategy with the twenty years of data the simulation records for them. It develops systems thinking (tracing how one change ripples through many variables), scientific enquiry (predict, observe, record, explain), quantitative data analysis of a real time-series, and evidence-based decision-making, all tied directly to the Introduction to Environmental Science.

orient.objective: Manage a wetland ecosystem over 20 years and explain how conservation, development and pollution decisions shape its biodiversity, water quality and resilience — including consequences that appear only years later.
orient.courseLink: Environmental Science, High School — Introduction to the course. This activity previews the big ideas the whole course is built on: food webs and energy flow, carrying capacity and limiting factors, nutrient pollution, invasive species, ecosystem resilience, and the trade-offs between human needs and a healthy environment.
successCriteria: Describe how one management decision changes several connected parts of a wetland food web, not just one thing.
Use your own 20-year data to explain a delayed consequence — such as fertiliser causing a fish die-off years later.
Judge which kind of strategy builds ecosystem resilience, using evidence from how your wetland survived the final drought.
orient.mission: You are the new manager of Marisma de Veralba, a Mediterranean wetland. You have 20 years and a yearly budget. Farmers want more land, developers want housing, and tourism brings in money — but the wildlife needs clean water and habitat. Keep the ecosystem alive and biodiverse enough to survive a brutal five-year drought at the end.
steps: Read the wetland food-web diagram, then predict what one risky decision will do.
Manage the wetland: each year pick up to three actions within your budget.
Every year you complete logs its actions, any event, and your key indicators to your Investigation Record.
Explain a pattern from your data, apply it to a real town's decision, then take the Knowledge Check.
Generate your Learning Evidence to hand in.
orient.realLife: Real wetlands are life-support: they filter the water you drink, buffer floods, store carbon, and feed fisheries. The fertiliser-to-algae-to-dead-water chain in this game is the exact process behind real 'dead zones' that close beaches and collapse fisheries around the world — so the trade-offs you weigh here are ones real towns and governments face now.

predict.prompt: In your first years you grow the budget fast by expanding farming and using more fertiliser. Over the following years, what is most likely to happen to the wetland's water quality and fish?
predict.hint: Fertiliser is a nutrient. Think about what nutrients feed in the water, what an algal bloom does to oxygen — and how long that takes to show up.

options.label: Water quality drops after a delay as nutrients feed algae, and fish decline later
Water quality and fish improve straight away because plants grow faster
Nothing changes — farming happens on land, not in the water
Fish increase permanently because fertiliser adds nutrients they eat

investigate.title: Manage the Marisma for 20 Years
investigate.lede: Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, click things to inspect them. Each year choose up to three actions, press Plan year, predict, then Confirm. Every year you complete logs its actions, any event, and your biodiversity, water quality and resilience to your Record below. Reach Year 20 to face the final drought.

record.intro: Each year you complete logs itself here automatically — actions, any event, and your key indicators — so you never retype data the simulation already produced.
record.emptyText: No years logged yet. Play a year in the simulation (choose actions → Plan year → Confirm) to log your first row.

explain.prompt: Look at your Investigation Record. Pick ONE clear pattern across your years — for example how biodiversity or water quality changed after a particular decision — and explain what caused it. If you can, point to a consequence that only appeared a few years after the decision that caused it.
explain.lede: Use the actual numbers from your own 20 years.
expectedPoints: Identifies a real trend from their own data (e.g. biodiversity rose after restoring habitat or removing the invasive species; water quality or fish fell after expanding farming/fertiliser).
Gives a cause-and-effect mechanism (fertiliser → more nutrients → algal bloom → less oxygen → fish die-off; or reduced pollution / restored habitat raised carrying capacity so populations recovered).
Recognises a DELAYED effect — the consequence lagged the decision by one or more years, or that pressures built up and compounded over time rather than acting instantly.

apply.prompt: A real coastal town wants to drain part of a nearby wetland for farmland and holiday homes, promising jobs and income now. Using what your simulation showed about trade-offs and delayed effects, give TWO reasons this could harm the ecosystem later, and suggest ONE thing the town could do to reduce the damage while still gaining some benefit.
apply.lede: Base each reason on something you actually saw happen in your wetland.
expectedPoints: Losing wetland area removes habitat, which lowers carrying capacity and biodiversity and makes the ecosystem less resilient.
Farming/housing adds nutrient runoff or reduces water, lowering water quality (algae, low oxygen, fish decline) — often as a delayed effect.
The town loses ecosystem services people depend on — flood protection, water filtration, carbon storage, fisheries or tourism.

A sensible mitigation: protect/restore part of it, add buffer strips or wildlife corridors, reduce fertiliser, improve wastewater treatment, limit water extraction, or phase the development — trading some short-term income for long-term resilience.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: What does the 'carrying capacity' of a population mean?

options.label: The largest population a habitat can support long-term, given food, space and conditions
The total number of different species in an ecosystem
How quickly a population can move through the water
The combined weight of animals a wetland can physically hold

knowledgeCheck.explain: Carrying capacity is the ceiling a habitat can sustain over time — set by limiting factors like food, space and water quality. Push a population above it and it falls back.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Fertiliser running off farmland into a wetland most directly causes which chain of events?

options.label: More nutrients → algal bloom → less oxygen → fish die (often after a delay)
Fewer nutrients → clearer water → more fish immediately
More oxygen → more algae → more fish forever
No change, because fertiliser stays locked in the soil

knowledgeCheck.explain: This is eutrophication: extra nutrients feed algae, the bloom then decays and strips oxygen from the water, and fish die — usually a year or more after the pollution, which is why it is easy to miss.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Match each management action to its main effect on the wetland.

pairs.right: Nutrient pollution and later algal blooms
Habitat lost and more water demand

knowledgeCheck.explain: Every decision moves several connected variables at once — that is what makes managing an ecosystem a balancing act rather than a single lever.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Two wetlands face the same severe five-year drought. Which is more likely to come through it with its wildlife intact?

options.label: The one with high biodiversity, clean water and protected water reserves
The one managed only for the maximum short-term income
The one left with a single dominant species and a drained marsh
Both fail equally, because droughts are completely random

knowledgeCheck.explain: Resilience is the ability to absorb a shock and recover. Diversity, clean water and a water buffer give an ecosystem more ways to cope; a system optimised only for income is brittle.

rubric.note: You are graded out of the total marks, shown as a percentage.

criteria.label: Use of evidence
criteria.descriptor: Explain answer uses your own recorded 20-year data.

criteria.label: Scientific reasoning
criteria.descriptor: Apply answer links trade-offs and delayed effects to the real decision.

criteria.label: Communication
criteria.descriptor: Clear sentences and correct environmental-science terms.

aiMarkingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply) using the rubric and each question's expected_points. Copy auto_marked_score into knowledge_accuracy. For Explain, credit any genuine trend from the student's own recorded data plus a valid cause-and-effect mechanism, and award full marks only if a delayed/compounding effect is recognised. For Apply, accept any two reasonable harms and any one sensible mitigation. Accept scientifically valid alternative wording; do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Report the total, the percentage, one strength, one correction and one next step, all under 80 words.
